title: Sales Enablement Prospect Playbook: Positioning, Pricing, Competitive Brief, Case Studies & Security FAQ
author: Ava Chen
content:
Overview

This prospect-facing playbook consolidates Redwood Inference positioning and messaging, concise competitive talking points, a recommended pitch-deck outline, guardrails for pricing conversations, two short case studies, and a vendor-focused Security FAQ for enterprise prospects. Use this document for pre-sales discovery, AE enablement, and sales engineering briefings.

Use cases and target personas

- Primary personas: VP/Director of Engineering, ML Platform Lead, Product Managers building LLM features, CTOs evaluating inference economics.
- Typical prospect triggers: high token spend, inconsistent latency for generation/chat, regulatory or data residency needs, desire to standardize inference across cloud/private environments.

Key positioning pillars (elevator pitch)

- Developer-first production inference: Redwood provides a unified runtime, API, and tooling so engineering teams ship LLM features with predictable latency, cost, and reliability.
- Deployment flexibility: Hosted API for fast time-to-value, Reserved Dedicated pools for predictable throughput, and Private deployments (VPC/on-prem) for regulated workloads.
- Cost-aware performance controls: Intelligent batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization profiles that drive measurable unit-cost improvements without sacrificing quality.
- Reliability & graceful degradation: Smart routing and automatic fallbacks keep production apps online during capacity or region disruptions.

Core messaging by persona

- VP Engineering / CTO: Focus on predictable unit economics, SLA-backed Dedicated options, and developer velocity. Emphasize the platform's ability to reduce operational overhead vs. building in-house inference.
- ML Platform Lead: Highlight model lifecycle features (version pinning, canary rollouts), model catalog with verified performance profiles, and observability (per-route token cost, latency traces).
- Product Manager / PM: Emphasize improved UX: streaming responses, function/tool calling, and structured output support with lower latency and stable performance.
- Security/Compliance Manager: Stress Private deployment options, KMS/HSM integrations, audit logs, and configurable data residency.

Competitive brief (one-paragraph summaries + quick matrix)

- Public cloud managed endpoints (AWS SageMaker, GCP Vertex AI): Strengths: integrated cloud infra, large partner ecosystems. Weaknesses: higher per-request cost for interactive workloads, less opinionated inference optimizations for LLM-scale serving.
- API-first LLM providers: Strengths: simplicity and breadth of models. Weaknesses: limited private deployment options and fewer controls for unit-cost optimization.
- Inference infrastructure vendors/self-hosted runtimes: Strengths: deep control and potential cost savings at scale. Weaknesses: heavy engineering burden and slower time-to-value.

Quick competitor matrix (high-level)

Dimension | Redwood Inference | Cloud Managed | API-first LLMs | Self-hosted runtimes
---|---:|---:|---:|---:
Time-to-value | High (hosted API) | High | High | Low
Cost controls | Strong (batching, caching, quantization) | Medium | Low | High (but ops cost)
Private deployments | VPC/on-prem available | Limited | Rare | Yes
SLA & enterprise support | Yes (Dedicated + Enterprise) | Varies | Paid tiers only | Depends

Pitch deck: recommended slide flow (10-12 slides)

1. Title & hook: one-liner that maps to prospect pain (latency, cost, reliability).
2. Problem: short data-backed examples (e.g., % of API calls that exceed latency SLO, or average token cost trending).
3. Market & why inference matters: positioning of serving vs. model ownership.
4. Redwood solution overview: runtime, control plane, and deployment modes.
5. Demo / architecture diagram: typical flow for Hosted vs. Dedicated vs. Private.
6. Performance benchmarks: tokens/sec, median p95 latency, and cost-per-1k tokens for representative workloads. (Include model names & instance shapes where relevant.)
7. Reliability & rollouts: canary/A-B, fallbacks and tracing hooks.
8. Security & compliance: KMS/HSM, audit logs, network topology options.
9. Pricing options & TCO comparison: hosted usage, committed Dedicated, Private license + support.
10. Customer case studies & ROI: short quantified bullets.
11. Implementation plan & timeline: discovery, pilot, roll to prod.
12. Call to action: pilot proposal and next steps.

Pricing guidance (talking points and guardrails)

- Pricing pillars: hosted usage (pay-as-you-go tokens/embedding units), Dedicated (monthly/annual committed capacity), Private (platform fee + support). Always frame pricing as a function of unit economics (cost per API call / cost per active user).

- Hosted (quick reference):
  - Recommend anchoring on 3-month usage trends during discovery to estimate hosted cost.
  - Typical objections: "We need lower cost" -> counter: show batching/caching/quantization levers and expected % savings.

- Dedicated (quick reference):
  - Ideal for predictable throughput and lower marginal token cost; requires a commitment window.
  - Offer a proof-of-concept (4-8 weeks) with capacity sizing based on peak RPS and model choice.

- Private (quick reference):
  - Recommended for regulated environments or when customers require full network isolation. Structure as license + implementation + annual support.

Simple pricing decision checklist (for AEs):

1. Is data residency, network isolation, or regulatory control required? -> Private.
2. Does the customer have predictable high-volume steady traffic? -> Dedicated.
3. Is the customer early-stage or experimenting? -> Hosted.

Case studies (short, prospect-facing)

1) FinTech payments assistant - Global bank
- Situation: Bank needed 99th percentile response times <250ms for fraud triage chat and to limit monthly inference cost growth.
- Outcome: Moved from cloud-managed endpoints to Redwood Dedicated; implemented KV caching for common prefixes and batching for background re-ranking jobs. Result: 3x improvement in throughput, p95 latency reduced from 420ms to 180ms, and 28% reduction in monthly inference spend.

2) Vertical SaaS knowledge assistant - Mid-market SaaS
- Situation: Rapid productization of a knowledge assistant required consistent developer experience across hosted and private environments for enterprise customers.
- Outcome: Adopted Redwood Hosted for initial launch, then migrated enterprise customers needing isolation to Private with the same API and rollout controls. Result: 6-week time-to-market for MVP, smoother enterprise onboarding with standard integrations (SAML + SCIM) and per-customer RBAC.

Security FAQ for prospects (concise answers)

Q: What deployment options support regulatory or data residency requirements?
A: Redwood supports Private deployments (VPC and on-prem options). We provide a customer-managed control plane and integrations with KMS/HSM for key custody.

Q: How is customer data isolated in Dedicated vs Hosted?
A: Dedicated capacity provides isolated GPU pools and per-tenant routing; customer data is logically separated and we offer contractual controls for data processing. Hosted environments are multi-tenant but implement strict access controls and tenant separation; for regulated workloads we recommend Dedicated or Private.

Q: What audit and logging capabilities are available?
A: Per-request audit logs, API access logs, model versioning history, and optional long-term retention packages that integrate with customer SIEM via S3/Cloud Storage or syslog.

Q: How do you manage keys and encryption?
A: We integrate with common KMS providers (AWS KMS, Google KMS, Azure Key Vault) and support customer-managed keys for Private deployments. For higher assurance, HSM integrations are available under enterprise agreements.

Q: What is the incident escalation process?
A: Public customers get standard incident notifications via status.redwood.ai. Enterprise customers with Dedicated/Private SLAs receive a documented runbook, 24x7 on-call support contacts, and quarterly review cadences.

Sales playbook: discovery questions & objection handling

- Discovery prompts:
  - What are your 95th/99th percentile latency targets for conversational flows?
  - How predictable is your traffic (diurnal cycles, burst patterns)?
  - Do you have regulatory or data residency constraints?
  - What models are you using today and what quality regressions can you tolerate?
  - What is your current monthly spend on inference?

- Objection handling examples:
  - "We can self-host cheaper" -> Acknowledge potential for lower raw infra cost, then quantify ops, engineering time, and risk (deploying updates, kernel optimizations, rolling upgrades). Offer TCO model comparing 12-month total cost.
  - "We need more control over latency" -> Offer Dedicated + SLA, and propose pilot with instrumentation to measure p95/p99 under representative load.
  - "Security concerns with multi-tenant hosted" -> Recommend Dedicated or Private; provide Security FAQ and propose an architecture review with security engineering.

Assets & next steps for the AE/SE

- Available collateral: pitch-deck template, benchmark datasheet, Dedicated sizing calculator (spreadsheet), Security FAQ PDF, customer reference list, one-pager on deployment options.
- Suggested next steps: schedule architecture review with prospect (include SE and SRE), propose a 4-8 week pilot (scope, success metrics, and exit criteria), and prepare a tailored TCO estimate.

Appendix: Implementation timeline (example for pilot -> production)

1. Discovery & sizing (1-2 weeks): collect traffic patterns, models, latency targets.
2. Pilot setup (2-4 weeks): provision Hosted/Dedicated or Private staging, run representative load and evaluate SLOs.
3. Optimization (1-3 weeks): enable batching/caching/quantization profiles, tune autoscaling.
4. Rollout (2-6 weeks): canary deploy, integrate observability and cost-tracking, finalize SLA and support.

Notes

Keep messaging technical enough for engineering audiences but outcome-focused for execs. When possible, quantify benefits (latency improvements, % cost reduction, time-to-market). Always align pricing conversations against unit economics and provide clear migration paths between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.
